newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Quiet week seen for Asian stocks, Dow hits record.
newsitem.headline: Quiet week seen for Asian stocks, Dow hits record.

text.p: Asian stock markets are set for further subdued activity because of a holiday-shortened trading week ahead, brokers said.
Market players are likely to hold off major trading decisions until the New Year holidays are over, they said.
But a record-high close for the Dow Jones industrial average on Friday might inject some life into sluggish Asian bourses.
The Dow rose 14.23 points to end at 6,560.91, topping the previous all-time high of 6,547.79 set on November 25 and taking its recent rally to its eighth consecutive session.
Portfolio managers continued to snap up big, relatively safe stocks before the year-end, helping the index overcome weakness in the technology sector.
HONG KONG - Stocks are likely to see relatively quiet trade in the coming shortened trading week, with any rally led more by the retail sector than institutions, brokers said.
"It is likely to be a quiet week, but with possibly some futures-related buying on Monday," said James Osborn in institutional sales at ING Barings.
The Hang Seng Index closed at 13,404.14 on Friday. Over the week, the index climbed 272.73 points, or 2.08 percent.
The stock exchange will trade only during the morning session on Tuesday, close for the New Year holiday on Wednesday and resume normal trading the next day.
TOKYO - Foreign investors, often a driving force in long-term rallies on the Japanese stock market, are likely to turn more cautious in 1997, analysts say.
They said the yen's weakening against the dollar cuts the dollar-denominated value of Japanese equities, which might send the yen and stocks down into a double spiral in the short term.
"The double spirals (of falls in the yen and stocks) will likely continue in January, and the Nikkei could dive below 19,000 again," said Haruyoshi Mabuchi, chief strategist at Nikko Research Center.
On Friday, the Nikkei average of 225 leading shares closed at 19,369.04, compared with the previous week's close of 19,690.46.
BANGKOK - Thailand's SET Index is expected to remain weak on continuing market concerns about the economy, including a high current account deficit and disappointing exports.

"Local mutual fund managers aren't happy about the latest economic indicators released by the central bank on Thursday. They're worried about exports and (the) current account deficit," said Thanadech Mahapokai of Book Club Finance and Securities.
The SET index finished at 835.71 on Friday against 816.79 a week ago.
DHAKA - Bangladesh stocks suffered heavy losses as retail investors and dealers continued to sell throughout the week to avoid further losses in a falling market.
Share prices tumbled each session in absence of any fresh buying, triggering tension in the kerb market. Kerb market traders threatened to stop floor trade from Sunday if prices kept falling.
Brokers fear the market may get further jolts in the week ahead if kerb market traders stick to their threat.
The DSE benchmark index lost 317.7 points to close at 2,269 in the week ending Thursday.
JAKARTA - Brokers and analysts said the market was likely to be sluggish in the coming week because the Jakarta stock exchange will only be open on two days.
The bourse will be closed from December 30 to January 1.
"Many investors will be on holiday, and I think the market will only return to normal in mid-January," an analyst with a Japanese securities firm said.
On Friday, the Jakarta Composite Index closed at 637.43 points, against the previous week's 632.52 points.
KARACHI - Pakistani stocks are expected to be mixed due to continuing political unrest, when the market reopens on Sunday, dealers said.
"We do not expect a bullish sentiment," dealer Ali Raza said. "The political unrest would continue till February 3 general elections."

On Tuesday, the Karachi Stock Exchange 100-share index ended up 3.15 points, or 0.23 percent, at 1,375.55, compared to a close of 1,378.57 on December 19. The market was closed for local holidays on Wednesday and Thursday.
KUALA LUMPUR - Trading in the New Year holiday week should mirror the quiet activity of the previous week, dealers said.
For the week, the Composite Index of 100 large-capitalised stocks rose 5.94 points to 1,209.
Small-capitalisation stocks, which provided a bit of buying interest, despite a lacklustre blue-chip index, could give trading some spark, dealers said.

"In the last couple of days, we may have seen a bounce in the Second Board, but that doesn't mean much," said Leong Yoon Siang, of TA Securities' international division. "I don't think we're expecting anything to lead the market in the next week."
Malaysian markets are closed on Wednesday for the New Year holiday.
MANILA - The mood of the Philippines market mood will generally be positive in the two trading days of the coming week as fund managers return from their holidays, dealers said.
The Philippines bourse will be closed from Monday to Wednesday and trading resumes on Thursday.

"Everyone will be waiting for the realignment of portfolios. New market themes will have to be developed as investors look for growth sectors and this year's focus will likely be on consumer stocks," said Erwin Tan, research manager at Abacus Securities Corp.
The main index closed on Friday at 3,170.56, or 9.64 points down from the previous week's 3,180.20.
SEOUL - The South Korean bourse will be closed from December 28 to January 2, and open for abbreviated sessions on January 3 and January 4.
South Korean stocks fell heavily on Thursday and Friday after a series of crippling strikes took hold in response to the ruling party pushing through a controversial labour law.

The unrest is set to continue over the New Year period, further unsettling the nation's markets and hopes of sustaining a fragile economic recovery. A major one-day strike affecting banks is set for next Saturday.
The market finished the week at 651.22, down 49.65 points or 7.08 percent, from the previous Friday's 700.87.
SINGAPORE - Dealers said they expected interest in Singapore shares to remain muted in the coming week before Thursday's general election and the start of the new year.
"People are reserving their fire power for next year now," said one local dealer. "There's hardly anything to focus on besides the election. There's just no news."
The key Straits Times Industrials Index closed on Friday at 2,202.60, up 5.79 points over the previous week.
SYDNEY - Australian shares look set to continue higher in the near term after a stronger Wall Street market helped push Sydney to a record closing high on Friday.
The All Ordinaries index closed at 2,395.6, up 21.8 points over the week, a record closing level after reaching 2,392.7 on November 20.

"I think we will see similar light trade (in the coming week) although there could be some window dressing by institutions for the end of the second (fiscal) quarter," said Phillip Toop, a dealer at brokerage Lance Jones.
TAIWAN - Taiwanese share prices are expected to consolidate in a narrow range next week because of the New Year holiday mood, brokers said.
A lack of inspiring news in the market would also prevent players from trading actively, they said.
"Many investors have stepped to the sidelines before the New Year holiday comes. The market should be even more inactive next week," said Foremost Invsetment analyst Wang Jieh.
On Friday, the weighted index ended at 6,863.02, compared with 6,890.66 a week ago.
WELLINGTON - The New Zealand top-40 share index ended the holiday-shortened week almost unchanged at 2,350.42 and brokers doubt it will move too far in another truncated week ahead.
First NZ Capital broker David Price said he expected some end-of-year jockeying on Tuesday but little change in trend until December quarter inflation data on January 17.
